Let me analyze the failing verification in the `otherbSearch` method. The postcondition that fails is: ``` ensures 0<=p<=v.Length && p != 0 ``` The counterexample shows: `elem = 8168, v.Length = 1, v[0] = 8168`. In this case, `b = true` and `p = 0`. Let me trace through the code: - `binarySearch(v, elem)` is called. Since `v[0] = 8168 = elem`, binary search should return `p = 0` (the last index where `v[u] <= elem`). - Since `p != -1` (p = 0), we go to the else branch. - `b := v[0] == elem` → `b := true` - `p := p + if b then 0 else 1` → `p := 0 + 0 = 0` So `p = 0` and `b = true`. The postcondition requires `p != 0`, but `p = 0`. The issue is with the postcondition `p != 0`. This postcondition seems incorrect. The purpose of `otherbSearch` appears to be to find the insertion point (the first index where `v[w] > elem`), which can be 0 (if elem is less than all elements) or `v.Length` (if elem is >= all elements). Wait, looking more carefully at the postconditions: - `ensures 0<=p<=v.Length && p != 0` - `ensures b == (elem in v[0..v.Length])` - `ensures b ==> p (forall u::0<=u

v[u] v[w]>elem)` The `p != 0` condition doesn't make sense in general. If `elem` equals `v[0]`, then `p` should be 0 (pointing to the element), and `b` should be true. The constraint `p != 0` is simply wrong. The correct postcondition should be `0<=p<=v.Length` without the `p != 0` constraint. The `p != 0` was likely a mistake. Actually, wait. Let me reconsider. Maybe the intent was `p != -1`? No, that doesn't make sense either since `p` is redefined after the binary search. Looking at the logic: - If `binarySearch` returns -1 (elem not found, and all elements > elem), then `p = -1 + 1 = 0`. So `p = 0` is valid. - If `binarySearch` returns some index and `v[p] == elem`, then `p` stays the same. - If `binarySearch` returns some index and `v[p] != elem` (which means `v[p] > elem`... wait, no. Binary search returns the last index where `v[u] <= elem`. If `v[p] != elem`, then `v[p] < elem`... no wait, the binary search postcondition says `forall u :: 0<=u<=p ==> v[u]<=elem`. If `v[p] != elem`, then `v[p] < elem`. But that can't happen if the array is sorted and we're looking at the last position where `v[u] <= elem`... actually it can if there are duplicates. Wait, let me re-read the binary search postcondition: ``` ensures (forall u::0<=u<=p ==> v[u]<=elem) && (forall w::p v[w]>elem) ``` So `p` is the last index where `v[u] <= elem`, or -1 if no such index exists. In `otherbSearch`: - If `p == -1`: elem is less than all elements. `b = false`, `p = 0`. This makes sense: the insertion point is 0. - If `p != -1` and `v[p] == elem`: elem is found. `b = true`, `p` stays the same. - If `p != -1` and `v[p] != elem`: Since `v[p] <= elem` and `v[p] != elem`, we have `v[p] < elem`. But wait, can this happen? If `v[p] < elem`, then all elements at positions <= p are < elem, and all elements at positions > p are > elem. So elem is not in the array. `b = false`, `p = p + 1`. This is the insertion point. So the valid range for `p` in the return is `0 <= p <= v.Length`. The `p != 0` constraint is simply wrong. When `elem` is less than all elements, or when `elem == v[0]`, `p` can be 0. The fix is to remove `&& p != 0` from the postcondition, making it just `0<=p<=v.Length`. Now, what category is this? It's an `ensures` (postcondition) that is incorrect - it states something that the implementation cannot guarantee. The proof obligation type... The error is "a postcondition could not be proved on this return path" - this is a postcondition that the implementation can't satisfy. This isn't really initiation, preservation, or bridge in the loop sense. But among the three options, this is closest to a "bridge" issue - the implementation's final state doesn't satisfy the postcondition. Actually, it's more fundamentally that the postcondition itself is wrong. It's a method postcondition issue. The closest fit is "bridge" - the computation's result doesn't bridge to the stated postcondition.
